## Further Reading

Acito, A. A., Burks, J. J., & Johnson, W. B. (2009). Materiality decisions and the correction of accounting errors. *The Accounting Review*, *84*(3), 659–688. <https://doi.org/10.2308/accr.2009.84.3.659> A study of how more than 250 U.S. companies corrected the same operating lease accounting error between 2004 and 2006, either by restating their prior statements or by a less visible catch-up adjustment in the current period. Quantitative and qualitative materiality considerations explained much of the choice, but so did what other companies had done, which shows how much judgment goes into deciding how to present a correction.

Allee, K. D., & Yohn, T. L. (2009). The demand for financial statements in an unregulated environment: An examination of the production and use of financial statements by privately held small businesses. *The Accounting Review*, *84*(1), 1–25. <https://doi.org/10.2308/accr.2009.84.1.1> A study of small private businesses that no regulator requires to prepare financial statements: which of them prepare statements, which have them compiled, reviewed, or audited, and which use the accrual basis. Firms with audited statements had greater access to credit, and firms with accrual-based statements a lower cost of credit, which is the reason a bank asks a company like Charles River for statements prepared under GAAP.

Choudhary, P., Merkley, K. J., & Schipper, K. (2021). Immaterial error corrections and financial reporting reliability. *Contemporary Accounting Research*, *38*(4), 2423–2460. <https://doi.org/10.1111/1911-3846.12713> Large-sample evidence on errors that companies corrected without a restatement because they judged them immaterial to the statements that contained them. Such corrections became more common after about 2004, and they foreshadowed later errors, material weaknesses in internal control, and comment letters from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The paper is useful when you decide whether a small error that recurs every year deserves attention.

Hennes, K. M., Leone, A. J., & Miller, B. P. (2008). The importance of distinguishing errors from irregularities in restatement research: The case of restatements and CEO/CFO turnover. *The Accounting Review*, *83*(6), 1487–1519. <https://doi.org/10.2308/accr.2008.83.6.1487> The authors separate restatements that correct unintentional errors from those that correct intentional misstatements, which they call irregularities, and show that the two have very different consequences for companies and their executives. The distinction is the reason this case words every finding as what the records show rather than as what anyone intended.

Minnis, M. (2011). The value of financial statement verification in debt financing: Evidence from private U.S. firms. *Journal of Accounting Research*, *49*(2), 457–506. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-679X.2011.00411.x> Using a large proprietary database of private U.S. firms, the study finds that audited firms have a significantly lower cost of debt, that lenders place more weight on audited figures when they set the interest rate, and that accruals from audited statements predict future cash flows better. It explains why a bank may ask for a review or an audit before it sets the final terms of a loan.

Minnis, M., & Sutherland, A. (2017). Financial statements as monitoring mechanisms: Evidence from small commercial loans. *Journal of Accounting Research*, *55*(1), 197–233. <https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-679X.12127> Drawing on records of banks' requests for information from small commercial borrowers, the authors study when banks use financial statements to monitor a loan after making it. Banks requested statements for about half of the loans, more or less often depending on the borrower's credit risk, the length of the relationship, the collateral, and whether the borrower provided tax returns. A lender's interest in the statements continues long after the loan is made.

Tan, C. E. L., & Young, S. M. (2015). An analysis of "little r" restatements. *Accounting Horizons*, *29*(3), 667–693. <https://doi.org/10.2308/acch-51104> The paper documents "little r" restatements, in which a company corrects immaterial errors that have accumulated to a material amount by revising the prior-year figures in its current statements, without reissuing the earlier statements. Most of the companies that did so in 2009 to 2012 gave readers no explanation of why the errors occurred, a point to weigh when you write the note on the correction of the 2025 statements.
